title: The seven bridges of Königsberg
hook: A Sunday stroll puzzle that Euler turned into a whole new branch of maths.
peek: The Prussian city of Königsberg had seven bridges linking two islands and two riverbanks. People wondered if you could cross each bridge exactly once on a single walk. In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved you cannot, and founded graph theory doing it.
lede: The city of Königsberg sat on the River Pregel, with two islands and seven bridges joining them to the banks. Residents puzzled over whether a walk could cross every bridge exactly once. In 1736 the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler proved it was impossible, and the way he did it mattered more than the answer.

bullets.text: Euler ignored distances and street shapes. He treated each landmass as a point and each bridge as a line, and saw that only the pattern of connections mattered. That stripped-down picture is what mathematicians now call a graph.
Every time you pass through a place, you use one bridge in and one out. So a place with an odd number of bridges must be where you start or finish. Königsberg had four such places, two too many.
Euler's dots-and-lines picture grew into graph theory, now used for networks, circuits and maps. The four color theorem is one of its most famous problems.

Königsberg is now Kaliningrad, in Russia. Several bridges were lost in the Second World War or later replaced, and with today's layout a walk crossing each bridge once is possible, though it cannot end where it began.
The same habit of thinking in connections helps with puzzles like the Rubik's Cube, where every position is a point and every twist is a line, and the question becomes the shortest route.
A modern cousin asks for the shortest route that walks every street at least once and returns home. Delivery and road-gritting rounds can be planned this way.
